name: The Lp(a) Research Center
blurb: Lipoprotein(a): the inherited heart risk factor, how to test for it, and the race to treat it.
title: The Lp(a) Research Center
answer: Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), is a cholesterol carrying particle whose level is set mostly by your genes. High Lp(a) raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and aortic valve narrowing even when LDL cholesterol is well controlled. New drugs can cut Lp(a) by 80 to more than 95 percent, but none is approved yet, and in September 2026 the first outcome trial, of pelacarsen, did not show fewer heart attacks or strokes despite lowering Lp(a).

sections.heading: What it means for patients

explainer:
Most people know their LDL cholesterol. Few know their Lp(a), even though about one person in five has an elevated level. Lp(a) is an LDL-like particle with an extra protein, apolipoprotein(a), attached. Its level is 70 to 90 percent inherited, stays fairly constant through life, and barely responds to diet or exercise, which is why it can be high in fit, slim people with excellent LDL numbers.

High Lp(a) is a cause, not just a marker, of atherosclerotic heart disease and of calcific aortic valve stenosis, the stiffening and narrowing of the main valve leaving the heart. That has driven a wave of drug development. Antisense and small interfering RNA drugs switch off production of apolipoprotein(a) in the liver, an oral pill blocks the particle from forming, and gene editing aims at a one time fix.

The field has reached its decisive moment. Lowering Lp(a) in the blood is no longer the hard part; proving that lowering it prevents heart attacks, strokes and valve disease is. The first outcome trial, with pelacarsen, failed to show that in people already on optimal treatment. Larger trials of the siRNA drugs and the oral pill are still running. This center keeps a strict line between "lowers Lp(a)" and "proven to reduce events".

developments.text: Novartis announced that the phase 3 Lp(a)HORIZON trial of pelacarsen in 8,323 people with established cardiovascular disease and elevated Lp(a) did not meet its primary endpoint of reducing cardiovascular events, although Lp(a) levels fell.

A review in Current Atherosclerosis Reports summarised five late stage Lp(a) agents across three mechanisms: the antisense drug pelacarsen, three siRNA drugs (olpasiran, lepodisiran, zerlasiran) and the oral pill muvalaplin, with CRISPR gene editing (CTX320) in phase 1.
